searchDocs.title: Installation​
searchDocs.content: Add Vet to your wally.toml:  [dependencies] Vet = "imkylecat/vet@0.1.0"   Then run wally install.

searchDocs.title: Your first schema​
searchDocs.content: local Vet = require(ReplicatedStorage.Packages.Vet) local Username = Vet.string():min(3):max(22) Username:parse("kyle") --> "kyle" Username:parse("ky") --> errors: expected at least 3 characters, got 2   Every schema starts from a constructor on Vet and is narrowed by chaining refinements. Refinements return a new schema, so a base schema is safe to share:  local Base = Vet.string() local Short = Base:max(10) local Long = Base:min(50) -- Base itself stays unconstrained

searchDocs.title: parse and safeParse​
searchDocs.content: parse returns the value and throws when validation fails. Use it when a failure is a bug worth surfacing.  safeParse never throws. Use it for data you do not control — remote arguments, DataStore reads, HTTP responses:  local result = Username:safeParse(input) if result.success then print(result.value) -- typed as string else for _, issue in result.issues do warn(issue.message) end end   Luau narrows on result.success, so result.value is only reachable once you have checked it.  Every refinement runs before the result is returned, so issues describes each failure rather than stopping at the first.

searchDocs.title: Inferring types​
searchDocs.content: Vet.infer extracts the type a schema parses to, so the schema stays the only place your field types are written down:  local User = Vet.object({ name = Vet.string():min(3), nickname = Vet.string():optional(), }) type User = Vet.infer<typeof(User)> --> { name: string, nickname: string? }   It works on every schema, including nested objects and arrays.  Vet.infer is a user-defined type function, so it runs during analysis and costs nothing at runtime. It needs a Luau version that supports user-defined type functions — in editors that means enabling the new type solver.

searchDocs.title: Issue​
searchDocs.content: </> interface Issue { path: {string | number}-- Location of the failure inside the value message: string-- Human-readable description of the failure }

searchDocs.title: Result<T>​
searchDocs.content: </> type Result<T> = { success: true, value: T } | { success: false, issues: {Issue} } Returned by safeParse. Narrow it with if result.success then to get a typed result.value.

searchDocs.title: infer<S>​
searchDocs.content: </> type infer<S> = thevaluetypeproducedbyschemaS Extracts the type a schema parses to, so a schema can be the single source of truth for both validation and types. local Username = Vet.string():min(3) type Username = Vet.infer<typeof(Username)> --> string local Nickname = Vet.string():optional() type Nickname = Vet.infer<typeof(Nickname)> --> string? Given a union of schemas, the result is the union of what each one parses to: Vet.infer<StringSchema | NumberSchema> is string | number. This is a user-defined type function, so it runs during analysis and costs nothing at runtime. It requires a Luau version that supports user-defined type functions.

searchDocs.title: objectOutput<S>​
searchDocs.content: </> type objectOutput<S> = therecordtypeashapeofschemasparsesto Maps { name: StringSchema, age: NumberSchema } to { name: string, age: number }. Used to type the result of Vet.object, so the shape you pass in is the only place the field types are written down. The property walk duplicates the one in Vet.infer because a type function cannot call another type function.

searchDocs.title: UuidVersion​
searchDocs.content: </> type UuidVersion = "v4" | "v5" | "v6" | "v7" | "v8" Versions accepted by Vet.uuid and Vet.guid. Version 4 is random, 5 is name-based, 6 is reordered time, 7 is Unix epoch time, and 8 is custom.

searchDocs.title: UuidOptions​

searchDocs.title: uuid​
searchDocs.content: </> Vet.uuid( options: UuidOptions?-- Pass { version = "v4" } to pin the version ) → StringSchema Creates a schema that accepts a UUID: 8-4-4-4-12 hexadecimal digits, in either case, carrying a version of 1 to 8 and an RFC 9562 variant. local Id = Vet.uuid() local SessionId = Vet.uuid({ version = "v7" }) Id:parse("01912d68-783e-7cc0-a2f0-5f8b1d3e9a7c") --> ok SessionId:parse("6f9619ff-8b86-4d11-b42d-00cf4fc964ff") --> errors: expected a v7 uuid, got v4 Because the version and variant are checked, the nil UUID and the max UUID are both rejected. Use Vet.guid when you only care about the layout. The result is a plain StringSchema, so :optional(), :default() and Vet.infer behave exactly as they do for any other string.

searchDocs.title: Errors
searchDocs.content: Type	Description"unknown uuid version ..."	Thrown when `options.version` is not v4 to v8

searchDocs.title: guid​
searchDocs.content: </> Vet.guid( options: UuidOptions?-- Pass { version = "v4" } to pin the version ) → StringSchema Creates a schema that accepts a GUID: the same 8-4-4-4-12 layout asVet.uuid, optionally wrapped in braces, with no variant requirement. local Id = Vet.guid() Id:parse("{6F9619FF-8B86-D011-B42D-00CF4FC964FF}") --> ok Id:parse("6f9619ff-8b86-d011-b42d-00cf4fc964ff") --> ok This is the shape HttpService:GenerateGUID returns, which is braced and uppercase by default. Values Microsoft produced do not always follow the RFC variant rule, so only the layout is enforced unless you pass a version.

searchDocs.title: Errors
searchDocs.content: Type	Description"unknown guid version ..."	Thrown when `options.version` is not v4 to v8

searchDocs.title: object​
searchDocs.content: </> Vet.object( shape: S-- Table mapping field names to schemas ) → ObjectSchema<Vet.objectOutput<S>> Creates a schema that validates a table field by field. The field types come from the shape, so the schema is the only place they are declared. local User = Vet.object({ name = Vet.string():min(3), nickname = Vet.string():optional(), }) type User = Vet.infer<typeof(User)> --> { name: string, nickname: string? }
